Borrowed from Medieval Latin abductor, from abdūcō + -tor.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin abrasiōnem (“a scraping”).

From Medieval Latin accessorius, as in the phrase accessorium sequitur principale (“the accessory follows the principal”). Possibly influenced by accidens (“falling down, something unfortunate happening”).
Inherited from Old French acquiter, from Medieval Latin acquitāre, adquietāre (“to pay a debt”), from ad- + quitare (“to set free”), from Late Latin quietāre.

parole.significato: activity (something to do for educational, recreational, or other purposes)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin āctīvitās. By surface analysis, actif + -ité.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin adaptātiōnem, from Latin adaptō (“to fit, adjust, modify; to adapt, fit or adjust to”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin adhērentem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin adhaesivus.

Compare Aragonese, Asturian, Extremaduran, and Spanish adiós; Catalan adeu; Dutch ajuus; English and Occitan adieu; German tschüss; Greek αντί
Borrowed from Medieval Latin agglomerātiō. By surface analysis, agglomérer + -ation.

parole.significato: a young apple tree or pear tree
parole.testo: From Old French aigrun, from Medieval Latin acrumen.
Inherited from Old French alambic
From Old French alkimie, borrowed from Medieval Latin alchēmia.

parole.significato: an alchemist; one who practices alchemy
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French alquemiste, from Medieval Latin alchemista.
Variant of alchimille, from Middle French alchimille, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin alchimilla.

parole.significato: alcohol, especially domestic, medical, methylated spirits
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin alcohol, from Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin algorismus, influenced by Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρῐθμός (ărĭthmós).
Inherited from Middle French allocacion, from Medieval Latin allocātiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin alternativus, from alternatus, perfect participle of alterno, from Classical Latin alter (“other”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin amalgamātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin amalgama.

parole.significato: ambidextrous (having equal ability with both hands)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ambidexter (literally “right-handed on both sides”), from ambi- + dexter (whence French dextre).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin amidum, from Latin amylum, from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon). Compare Spanish almidón, Greek άμυλο (ámylo), Hebrew עמילן (amilan).
From Old French amiral etc., from Medieval Latin amiralis, from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”) + -alis (“-al”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”). Doublet of amande and mandorle.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin anacardus, from Latin anacardium, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “on, upon”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”).
Inherited from Middle French ancolie, anquelie, aquelée, anquelée, angorie, argorie, from the obscure Medieval Latin aquilegia which became translingual Aquilegia.

parole.significato: native or inhabitant of Anjou, a former province of France (previously a county, duchy and the associated House of Anjo…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Andegāvīnus, from Latin Andegāvum, from Andecāvī.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Anglicānus, from Latin anglicus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin annuitātem, from Latin annuus (“annual”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin antilops, itself borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀνθόλοψ (anthólops).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin approbātīvus.
Inherited from Middle French apuyer, Old French apoiier, borrowed from Medieval Latin *appodiāre, from Latin podium. Compare Spanish apoyar, Portuguese apoiar, Italian appoggiare.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin armistitium, from Latin arma (“weapons”) and statio (“immobility”) (compare solstitium). Cognate with Italian armistizio, Spanish armisticio.

Inherited from Middle French armee, from the feminine past participle of the verb armer; first attested in French circa 1370 (except in Anglo-Norman), borrowed through Anglo-Norman from Medieval Latin armāta (“armed force”), the neuter plural form of the past participle of Latin armō (“to arm”), fro
Borrowed from Medieval Latin attribūtum.
From Medieval Latin authenticō.
Inherited from Old French auctorisier, from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre. Doublet of octroyer.

From Medieval Latin avunculāris, ultimately from Classical Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -āris (“-ar”). Inherited from Old French azur, borrowed from Medieval Latin azurium, from Arabic لَازُوَرْد (lāzuward, “lapis lazuli”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard, “lapis lazuli”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin baccalaureātus, from baccalaureus, an alteration of baccalārius (“young man aspiring to knighthood”) to resemble bacca laurī (“laurel berry”) (the ancient symbol of victory).

Inherited from Old French bacheler, bachelier, from Medieval Latin baccalaureus, a variant of baccalārius influenced by a folk etymology from bacca (“berry”), laurea (“laurel”), i.e. “crowned with berried laurels”, in reference to the fact that graduate students were crowned with those in the Middle

parole.significato: double boiler, bain-marie (hot water bath made out of two containers)
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin balneum Mariae (literally “Maria's bath”), a reference to the early alchemist Maria Prophetissima (also known as Mary the Jewess).

parole.significato: bundle of goods; packet tied and held together with string
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French balle (“large bundle, package”), from Old French bale (“rolled-up bundle, packet of goods”) and Medieval Latin bala, of Germanic origin. Cognate with English ball. Doublet of Etymology 1.
From Medieval Latin Balticus, from Late Latin Balthae (“dwellers near the Baltic sea”). See English Baltic.
From ban + -al, related to Medieval Latin bannālis, from bannus.
Inherited from Old French banlieue, from Medieval Latin banleuca. Compare Middle High German banmile, modern German Bannmeile.

parole.significato: the monopoly held by a feudal lord on sales of wine in their jurisdiction during a particular period of time
parole.testo: From ban + vin (“wine”), related to Medieval Latin bannus (“jurisdiction”).
From Medieval Latin barbarinus (“Berber, pagan, Saracen, barbarian”), from Latin barbaria (“foreign country”).
From Medieval Latin Basilidiānus, from Byzantine Greek Βασιλειδῐᾱνός (Basileidĭānós). By surface analysis, Basilide + -ien.

parole.significato: covered building, Civil reunion place open to the public
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ). Compare the inherited doublet basoche.
Inherited from Old French bombasin, ultimately from Medieval Latin bombyx, bambax, from Ancient Greek πάμβαξ (pámbax, “cotton”).
From Medieval Latin bladona.
Inherited from Old French bestiaire, borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium, from Latin bēstia.

parole.significato: a bifurcation, where two roads etc. part or meet
parole.testo: From bifurquer + -tion, Medieval Latin bifurcus (“two-pronged”).

parole.significato: A log or hunk of wood
parole.testo: From Old French bille (“stick of wood”), from Medieval Latin billa, billia, from Gaulish *belyos (“tree”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolyo- (“leaf”).

From Medieval Latin blondus, of Germanic origin: probably from Frankish *blund (“a mixed color between golden and light-brown”), from Proto-Germanic *blundaz (“mixed, blinding”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. Compare Italian biondo, Occitan blon.
Inherited from Middle French bordel, from Old French bordel, from Medieval Latin bordellum (“brothel, small hut”).

parole.significato: bollard such as those used to restrict automobiles off a pedestrian area
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French bontie, bodne, from Medieval Latin (Merovingian) bodina, butina (“limit, boundary”), a Celtic/Transalpine Gaulish borrowing, from Proto-Celtic *bonnicca (“boundary”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom, base”), see also *bundos.
Inherited from Old French bouffer, originally "to puff up," from Medieval Latin buffa, itself echoic of puffing out cheeks.

Inherited from Middle French bourdon (“honeybee, bumblebee”), from Old French bordon (“bumblebee, drone, beetle, insect”), from Medieval Latin burdō (c. C.E. 1000), first recorded in the Homilies of King Ælfric, glossed by Old English dora (“bumblebee”). Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Frankish *
Inherited from Old French borse, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa, “hide”).
From Middle French brueil, bruil, bruel, from Old French, from Medieval Latin brogilus (“fenced-in forest; game reserve”) (circa 800), Gaulish *brogilos.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin brūtālis (“savage, stupid”), from brūtus (“dull, stupid”). See brut and -al.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin būbō, from Ancient Greek βουβών (boubṓn, “groin, swelling”).
Inherited from Old French bugle, probably borrowed from Medieval Latin bugula, probably related to Late Latin bugillō (compare bouillon).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Bulgarus, from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ, “Bulgarian”). Doublet of bougre.

Inherited from Middle French bâtard, from Old French bastard (“child of a nobleman by a woman other than his wife”), from Medieval Latin bastardus (“illegitimate child”), from Proto-Germanic *banstuz, *bunstuz (“a bond”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie, bind”) + -ard. parole.significato: Beghard, Beguin (religious laymen living in semimonastic communities in imitation of the Beguines)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French beguin, from Medieval Latin beguina, said to be taken from the name of Lambert le Bègue, "Lambert the Stammerer." For the surname, see bègue (“stammering”).
From Medieval Latin b molle (“B flat”, literally “soft B”); the "flat" symbol looks like a small b, so this distinguishes it from the letter b.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin beneficiārius. By surface analysis, bénéfice + -aire.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cabbala, from Hebrew קַבָּלָה (kabalá, “Jewish mysticism”, literally “something received”).

parole.significato: calamine, form of zinc oxide formed as a byproduct of sublimation
parole.testo: FromMedieval Latin calamīna, from Latin cadmī̆a, ultimately from Ancient Greek Κᾰδμείᾱ (Kădmeíā), from Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming related substances”).
* Borrowed from Medieval Latin calefactorium.

Inherited from Middle French kamaheu, from Old French camaü (“precious stone, treasure”), of obscure origin. Compare Medieval Latin camaeus (probably of confluence with the older forms) also of unknown origin, and English cameo.

From Old French conopé, conope (later altered in form and meaning based on Medieval Latin canāpēum, alteration of canōpēum (“mosquito net”)), itself from Latin cōnōpēum (“seat with a canopy”), from Ancient Greek κωνωπεῖον (kōnōpeîon), from κώνωψ (kṓnōps, “mosquito”). Cognate with English canopy.

Inherited from Middle French kanete (“vase, pitcher for serving beer”), a diminutive (with suffix -ette) of Medieval Latin cana, canna (“can, jug, vessel”), from Frankish *kanna (“jug, pitcher, can”), from Proto-Germanic *kannǭ (“tankard, mug, can”), from Proto-Indo-European *gandʰ-, *gan- (“a vesse

parole.significato: treaty, convention; especially a treaty regarding the rights of nationals of one party with respect to the government o…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin capitulātiōnem. By surface analysis, capituler + -ation.

parole.significato: to surrender; to capitulate (to give oneself up into the power of another)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin capitulāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin carcanum (“collar”), the etymology of which is unknown.

parole.significato: card (a machine for disentagling the fibres of wool prior to spinning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cardō, from Latin carduus. Doublet of cardon and chardon.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cāritātīvus, from Latin caritas (“charity, dearness”).

parole.significato: carmine, crimson (having a deep, slightly bluish red colour)
parole.testo: Possibly from Medieval Latin *carminium, from Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz, “crimson, kermes”) (from Sanskrit कृमिज (kṛmija, “produced by worms”), from कृमि (kṛ́mi, “worm, insect”)), plus or with influence from Latin minium. Or, from a contraction of Old French carmesin, from Spanish carmesí.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin carminativus.
From Middle French Carolinge, from Medieval Latin Carolingus, from Germanic.
Inherited from Middle French carobe, from Medieval Latin carrubium, from Arabic خَرُّوب (ḵarrūb).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin chartulārium.
Inherited from Old French carvi, borrowed from Medieval Latin carvi, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā). Doublet of chervis.

Inherited from Middle French casserolle. By surface analysis, casse (“container, recipient”) + -erole (diminutive suffix), a form of -ole lengthened with -er-. From Medieval Latin Cathari, from Ancient Greek καθαρός (katharós, “pure”).

From Medieval Latin censivus and French recensement.

parole.significato: the division of the produce of land due by a tenant farmer to the feudal lord possessing the land
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin campartum, from campus + pars.

From chandelle + -ier, or from Medieval Latin candelārius. Compare Catalan candeler, Italian candelaio, Spanish candelero.

Inherited from Middle French chapelle, from Old French chapele, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin cappella, diminutive of cappa.

parole.significato: chicory (Cichorium intybus (“common chicory”) or Cichorium endivia)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French cicoree (probably later influenced by Italian cicoria), borrowed from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin *cichōria, from Latin cichōrium, from Ancient Greek κιχώριον (kikhṓrion).
From Medieval Latin cifra (“zero”), from Andalusian Arabic صِفر (ṣifr, “empty”). Doublet of zéro.

From Old French clause, borrowed from Medieval Latin clausa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin claustrālis.
From Medieval Latin clāvicymbalum (compare Italian clavicembalo), from clāvis (“key”) + cymbalum (“dulcimer, cymbal”).

parole.significato: bell (metal apparatus used to produce sound)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin clocca, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (see also Welsh cloch, Old Irish cloc), ultimately imitative. Related to Old English clucge, Low German Klock (“bell, clock”), German Glocke, Swedish klocka.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coalitiōnem, from Latin coalitus (“fellowship, communion”).

Latinate learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cogitātiōnem (“act of pondering; reflection”), supplanting or reshaping variant forms from Middle French cogitatiun, Old French cogitaciun, cogitacion, from Vulgar Latin cōgitātiōnem; compare Middle English cogitacioun, English cogitation. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin commēnsālis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin comminatorius.
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin commissiōnārius, from Latin commissiō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin communia, neuter plural of communis.
From Medieval Latin compāscuitās, from compāscuus + -itās.
Inherited from Middle French compatible, from Medieval Latin compatibilis.

parole.significato: to concern (be concerned with, be associated with)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French concerner, borrowed from Medieval Latin concernere (“I distinguish, have respect to”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- + cernō (“distinguish”).

parole.significato: accord, agreement, accordance, concurrence, consonance, concord
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin concordantia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin conditiōnālis (“conditional”), from conditiō (“condition”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin confrontātiō.
From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnsecūtīvus, from Latin cōnsecūtus (“followed up”), from Latin cōnsequor (“to travel”).
From contre + point, based on Medieval Latin contrapunctus.

An haplology of Middle French contrerole, a borrowing from Medieval Latin contrārotulum (“a counter-roll or register used to verify accounts”), from Latin contrā (“against, opposite”) + Latin rotulus, rotula (“roll, a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”).

Inherited from Old French contreroller, contreroler, from contrerole, from Medieval Latin contrarotulum (“a counter-roll or register used to verify accounts”), from Latin contrā (“against, opposite”) + Medieval Latin rotulus, Latin rotula (“roll, a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin copiāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cordiālis.
From Old French cormoran, from Medieval Latin corvus marīnus (literally “sea-raven”)
Inherited from Old French corneline.

parole.significato: corporeality (state of being or having a body)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French corporéité (first attested in 1482), borrowed from Medieval Latin corporeitātem.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin correspondēre.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin coteria, from Old English cot.
From Old French cortil (“garden, enclosure, small courtyard”), from Medieval Latin curtilis, from Latin curtus (“shortened, short”).
From Old French coutel (cf. modern couteau) + the suffix -ier; cf. also Medieval Latin cultellārius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin coxālis, from Latin coxa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin coincidentia.
From Middle French crane (14th c.), a borrowing from Medieval Latin crānium.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin credibilitātem, from Latin credibilis. By surface analysis, crédible + -ité.

parole.significato: to culminate (to come to an end)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin culmināre, from Latin culmen.

parole.significato: guardianship under which the ward is totally and permanently incapable
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cūrātēla, or formed from curateur + -elle, on the model of tuteur ~ tutelle.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin curativus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cursivus, from Latin cursus.

parole.significato: priest bearing the responsibility of a parish
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cūrātus.

parole.significato: pyx (small container used to hold the host)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin custōdia. Automotive sense ellipsis of vitre de custode f (literally “guard window”).

parole.significato: earwax (waxy substance secreted by the ear)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin caerūmen.
From Medieval Latin delphīnātus, from delphīnus (“dauphin”) + -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, dauphin + -at. Doublet of delphinat, dauphiné, and Dauphiné.
From Medieval Latin delphīnātus, from delphīnus (“dauphin”) + -ātus (suffix forming abstract nouns). Doublet of dauphinat and delphinat. By surface analysis, dauphin + -é (abstract noun suffix).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin de visu.

parole.significato: delphinal (of or relating to a dauphin)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin delphīnālis, from delphīnus + -ālis.

parole.significato: dandelion (plant, wild flower of the genus Taraxacum)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French dent de lion, calque of Medieval Latin dentis leōnis (“lion's tooth”).
From Medieval Latin dentālis, from Latin dēns (“a tooth”). By surface analysis, dent + -al.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diaphanus (“diaphanous”), from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) and φαίνω (phaínō, “show”).

parole.significato: dictionary (a list of words, usually arranged alphabetically and presented with definitions or translations)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French dictionnaire, borrowed from Medieval Latin dictiōnārium (“dictionary”), derived from Latin dictiō (“saying, speaking”) + -ārium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin diffāmātōrius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dislocātiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dispōnibilis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diversificātiōnem, from diversificātus, past participle of diversificō (“diversify”), from Latin diversus (“turned in different ways”) + faciō (“make, do”)
Borrowed from Medieval Latin diversificāre, by surface analysis, divers + ifier.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diversiōnem, from Latin divertō (“to divert”); see divert.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin domaniālis, from Latin dominium + -ālis.
Inherited from Middle French domiciliaire, from Medieval Latin domiciliārius. By surface analysis, domicile + -aire.

parole.significato: black hooded cloak worn by priests in winter
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dominō, from Latin dominus (“lord, master”), perhaps from a prayer formula such as "benedicamus domino". The development of the modern meaning is unclear, perhaps from the black color of the early domino tiles.
From Old French, borrowed from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from dōs, dōtis, and influenced by the verb douer.

parole.significato: customs (an authority responsible for controlling the flow of goods to and from a country)
parole.testo: Attested in Old French in 1281 as dohanne with the meaning “building where the rights of entry and exit of goods are earned” (Angevin Archives of Naples). In 1441 in the Middle French form doana (“rights of entry and exit of goods”). Borrowed from Sicilian Medieval Latin doana, dovana (attested from
Borrowed from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).
Calque of Medieval Latin dūra māter.

parole.significato: decadence (state of moral or artistic decline or deterioration)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin decadentia, from decadēns, present participle of decadō (whence the verb déchoir), from de- + cadō (“to fall”). Doublet of déchéance, naturally inherited from the same Latin root.

parole.significato: to decant, to clarify, to settle
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēcīsīvus.
From Medieval Latin dēfalcō (“cut or lop off”), from Latin dē (“off”) + falx (“sickle, scythe, pruning hook”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēfēnsīvus.
Inherited from Middle French democratie, from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēpūrāre, from pūrus (“pure”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin devolutiōnem, from Latin devolvō.
Calque of Medieval Latin aqua vītae (literally “water of life”).
Inherited from Middle French embrion, from Medieval Latin embryon, embrion, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, swell”).
From earlier enquent, from Middle French inquant, from Medieval Latin inquantum (“in as much as”).

parole.significato: Belgian endive (edible chicory bud of Cichorium intybus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French endive, endivie, andive, indivie, from Medieval Latin endivia or Italian indivia~endivia, from Byzantine Greek ἐντύβιον (entúbion), from Latin intibus (which see). The ultimate source is likely Semitic.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin entitātem.

Inherited from Middle French esclave, from Old French esclave (12th c.), a borrowing from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”). Doublet of slave. Chiefly a learned word, therefore not generally developed regularly into éclave, though this form is attested in Early Moder
Metathesized from estargon, from targon, borrowed from Medieval Latin tarcon, altarcon, from Arabic طَرْخُون (ṭarḵūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion), from δράκων (drákōn).

parole.significato: eccentricity (ratio between distances in a conic section)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin excentricitas. By surface analysis, excentrique + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin excentricus, from ex- (“away”) + centrum (“the centre”) + -icus. By surface analysis, ex- + centre + -ique.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin exhumāre, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).
From exploiter + -ation, Medieval Latin exploitationem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin expeditivus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin extravagantem.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin facētiōsus. By surface analysis, facétie + -eux.
From Medieval Latin fallibilis. See faillir + -ible.

Inherited from Old French farse, from Medieval Latin farsa, from the feminine perfect passive participle from Latin farciō (“to stuff”). Doublet of far. The theatre sense alludes to the pleasant and varied character of certain stuffed food items.
According to the TLFi, from Old French farinier, a borrowing from Medieval Latin farīnārius, from Latin farīna (“flour”). Equivalent to farine + -ier
From faucon + -erie, or from Medieval Latin falconaria.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin firmatūra. By surface analysis, fermer + -ure.
Uncertain, possibly from Medieval Latin faluppa (“bundle of wheat”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin fomentāre.

From Old French formatif, formative, from Medieval Latin formātīvus, from Latin fōrmātus + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘doing’ or ‘related to doing’). Fōrmātus is the perfect passive participle of fōrmō (“to form, to shape”); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to Ancie
Inherited from Old French forteresce, from Medieval Latin. Morphologically, from fort (“strong”) + -eresse (“-ess”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin frāternālis, from Latin frāternus, from frāter (“brother”) (whence frère).
From Medieval Latin fūmus terrae.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin funerālia. See also funéral, funéraire.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin febrilis, from Latin febris (whence fièvre).
From Old French felon, from Medieval Latin fellōnem. Compare Italian fellone.

parole.significato: to perform oral sex on (man or woman); to go down on
parole.testo: Possibly “going below the base” from Medieval Latin gamma ut, the note below the tonic in Guido D'Arezzo's six-note scale.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin gamma. Doublet of gamma.

Inherited from Middle French garenne, garanne, from Old French garenne, garanne, guarenne, from Medieval Latin warenna, itself of Germanic origin; from or related to Old High German warōn (“to be wary”) and werren (“to forbid”), through Proto-Germanic *warōną (“to heed, be careful”) and Proto-German
Inherited from Old French glose, from Medieval Latin glossa (“explanation of a difficult word”). See also English gloze (“to make a comment”).
Inherited from Middle French goutren, from Old French catran, from Medieval Latin catarannus, from Arabic قَطْرَان (qaṭrān). Form influenced by Middle French goutte (see French goutte).
From Medieval Latin gradālis (“dish”), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: to pardon, to issue a pardon to
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin grātiō, from Latin grātia. By surface analysis, grâce + -er.
From Medieval Latin graduālis, from Latin gradus (“step”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰradʰ-, *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”).

From Medieval Latin grātīcula, from Latin crāticula (“grating, grill”), from crātis (“hurdle; wickerwork”) (probably from Proto-Indo-European *kréh₂-tis (“fenced handiwork”)) + -cula (feminine form of -culus, a variant of -ulus (“diminutive suffix”)).
From Medieval Latin gratitudō.
Inherited from Middle French grave, borrowed from Latin gravis. Doublet of grief.

parole.significato: clerk of the court; registrar of the court, or similar role
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin graphiārius (“scribe, secretary”), from graphium (“stylus”). Compare greffe (“clerk's office”).
Named after the town of Gruyères, Switzerland, from Medieval Latin Gruerius, from Swiss French grue (“crane”).
From an alteration, likely via Medieval Latin, of Italian gattopardo (“serval”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin gȳrovagus (“wandering aimlessly”).
From Medieval Latin gabulum, of Celtic origin, from Gaulish gabalos, from Proto-Celtic *gablā (“fork”). Closely related to Old Norse gafl (English gable).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin habituālis.
From hache, hacher, via Medieval Latin hapia from Germanic.
Inherited from Middle French haye, from Old French haie, from Medieval Latin haga, from Frankish *haggju (whence English hedge) and/or related *hagō (whence English haw). Doublet of age and quai.
Inherited from Old French aleine, deverbal from alener (“to breathe”), from Medieval Latin anhēlō by metathesis. The h appeared around the 16th century under the influence of Latin hālō (“to blow”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin hermeticus, irregular derivation of Hermes Trismegistus, the god and mythological alchemist, said to possess a magic ability to seal treasure chests so that nothing could access their contents.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hōrārius.
Inherited from Middle French hospitalier, derived from hospital (whence modern hôpital) + -ier, in part after Medieval Latin hospitalarius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hypochondriasis.
From Medieval Latin iconographia. By surface analysis, icône + -o- + -graphie.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin identificāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin illegālis, from Latin legālis. Also il- + légal.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ileum, ileon, itself a derivative of Ancient Greek εἰλέω (eiléō).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin immātrīculāre.
From the Medieval Latin imperceptibilis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin importantia.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin incarcerāre, incarcerō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclusivus, from Latin inclusus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin incorruptibilitātem.

parole.significato: to incriminate (to accuse or bring criminal charges against)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin incrīmināre, from Latin crīmen (whence crime).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin individuum
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin indīviduālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin indurātiōnem.
From Old French influence, borrowed from Medieval Latin īnfluentia, from Latin īnfluēns (“flowing in”), present active participle of īnfluō (“flow into”), from in- (“in-”) + fluō (“flow”).

parole.significato: engineer (person qualified or professionally engaged in engineering)
parole.testo: Modified, based on the verb ingénier, from Old French engigneor, itself from engin or from Medieval Latin ingeniātōrem or ingeniārius (“one who makes or uses an engine”), from Latin ingenium (“an engine”), from in (“in”) + gignō, gignere (“to produce, cause”). The distinction was likely intentionall
From Medieval Latin *initiativus (“serving to initiate”), from Late Latin initiare (“to begin, Latin initiate”), from Latin initium (“beginning”), from ineo (“enter, begin”).

From Middle French, from Medieval Latin īnstallāre (“to install, put in place, establish”), from in- + stallum (“stall”), from Frankish *stall (“stall, position, place”), from Proto-Germanic *stallaz (“place, position”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to place, put, post, stand, be rigid”). Cogna
Inherited from Middle French insult m, probably borrowed from Medieval Latin insultus (“attack, assault”). By surface analysis, deverbal from insulter.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intēnsīvus, from Latin intēnsus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin interrogatōrium, from Late Latin interrogatōrius.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intimidāre (“to make afraid”), from timidus (“afraid, timid”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intuītiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French integral, borrowed from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer.

parole.significato: interest (great attention and concern from someone)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin interesse, from Latin interesse, from inter- + esse.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin invasivus.
Inherited from Old French inventif, from Medieval Latin inventivus, from Latin inventum.
Inherited from Middle French, borrowed from Medieval Latin investītūra. Displaced Old French envesture.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Scientific Latin iugulāris, from Latin iugulum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin iūrista.
From Medieval Latin jusquiamus, from Classical Latin hyoscyamus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑοσκύαμος (huoskúamos), from ὗς (hûs, “pig”) + κῠ́ᾰμος (kŭ́ămos, “bean”).
From Middle French chan, from Old French chan, from Medieval Latin chānus, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lacōnicus (“laconic”), from Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós).

From Old French lamproie, from Medieval Latin lamprēda, of uncertain origin: possibly from Late Latin lampetra, from a combination of lambō (“lick”) + petra (“stone”). Compare Spanish lamprea, Italian lampreda, Portuguese lampreia. However, see also Gaulish naupreda; naupreda is attested in the 5th
From Old French lardier, from Medieval Latin lardarium, from laridum (“lard”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin latīnizāre. By surface analysis, latin + -iser.

From Middle French lavande (ca. 1300), ultimately from Medieval Latin lavendula. The French form is said to derive from Italian lavanda, though the latter is attested significantly later. Alternatively it may be an independent dissimilation.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin laxativus.
Inherited from Middle French lectionnaire, borrowed from Medieval Latin lēctiōnārium (“lectionary”), derived from Latin lēctiō (“lesson”) + -ārium.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lenticulāris.

From Middle French, from Old French lastage (“ballast”), from Medieval Latin lestagium (“tax imposed on a ship's lading”), from Old English hlæst (“load, freight”), from Proto-Germanic *hlastą, *hlastuz (“load, burden”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”). Cognate with Old High Ger

parole.significato: to fire, to sack (to terminate the employment of)
parole.testo: From Middle French licencier, licensier, licentier, borrowed from Medieval Latin licentiō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin linguālis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin liquefactiō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin litra, from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, “a Sicilian coin, a measure of weight”).
From Medieval Latin Lōthariānus, from Lōtharius + -iānus.
From Medieval Latin Lūdovīciānus, from Lūdovīcus + -iānus. By surface analysis, Ludovic + -ien.

From Old French leitrun, from Medieval Latin lectrinum, from Late Latin lectrum, from lēctus, perfect passive participle of legō (“to read”). The noun was influenced by lu, past participle of lire, from a similar root.
From légal + -ité, or borrowed from Medieval Latin legalitātem, from Latin legalis. Compare also loyauté.

parole.significato: legend (story of unknown origin describing plausible but extraordinary past events)
parole.testo: From Old French legende, from Medieval Latin legenda, feminine of Latin legendus, gerundive of legēre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin lēgista.
From légitime, or borrowed from Medieval Latin legitimāre, from Latin legitimus.

Inherited from Middle French macis, from Old French macis, from late Medieval Latin macis, possibly a corruption of Latin macir (denoting a different red spice from India), from Ancient Greek μάκιρ (mákir, “macir”), an eastern loanword of unknown further origin.
Inherited from Old French macrocosme, from Medieval Latin macrocosmus, formed from Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós, “great, long”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”); macro- + -cosme.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin magnesia.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin maiōritās. By surface analysis, majeur + -ité.

Inherited from Middle French malle, from Old French male (“leather bag, leather or wooden travel-case”), from Frankish *malha (“leather bag”), from Proto-Germanic *malhō (“leather bag”), from Proto-Indo-European *molko- (“leather bag”). Cognate with Old High German malha, malaha (“leather bag”), Mid
Borrowed from Medieval Latin manipulāre.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin manufactūra (“making by hand”); from manū (“by hand”) + factūra (“act of making”).

1594, from Medieval Latin manuscriptum (“writing by hand”), from Latin manu (ablative of manus (“hand”)) + scriptus (past participle of scribere (“to write”)), calqued from a word of Germanic origin. Compare Middle High German hantschrift, hantgeschrift (c. 1450, “manuscript”), Old English handġewri
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin manūtentiō, from the past participle of manūteneō (“to maintain”).
From Old French manovre, from Medieval Latin manū opera (“handiwork”), a calque of Proto-West Germanic *handuwerk. Equivalent to main (“hand”) + œuvre (“work”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin marchasita et al., from Arabic مَرْقَشِيتَا (marqašītā).

parole.significato: Marennes (a Town and former commune in the department of Charente-Maritime, Nouvelle-Aquitaine)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Marennia, Maremnia, from a crossing between Latin maritimus (“sea shore”) and Latin marinus (“of or pertaining to the sea”). Influenced by Latin Maritimensis.

parole.significato: marginal (written in the margin of a book)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin marginālis, from Latin margō (whence marge).
From Old French majorane, from Medieval Latin maiorana.

Occurring in a 1086 Medieval Latin translation of the Domesday Book, from Old English mereswīn (“porpoise”), but probably reborrowed from another Germanic source cognate to the Old English word, from Old Frankish *mariswīn, Middle Dutch meerswijn, or Old Norse marsvín (“dolphin”), all ultimately fro

parole.significato: marshal (officer in the household of a medieval prince or lord)
parole.testo: From Middle French mareschal, from Old French mareschal, marescal, from Medieval Latin mariscalcus, from Frankish *marhskalk, from *marh (from Proto-Germanic *marhaz (“horse”)) + *skalk (from Proto-Germanic *skalkaz (“servant, knight”)). Compare also Italian maniscalco.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin masculīnitās.

parole.significato: minority (the state of being a minor; youth; period of life preceding adulthood)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin minoritās. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English minority. By surface analysis, mineur + -ité.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin minerālis, minerāle, from Latin minera.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin misericordiōsus . By surface analysis, miséricorde + -eux.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin modālis, from Latin modus (“mode”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin modernitās. By surface analysis, moderne + -ité.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sānctī moniālis (“nun”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin morganāticus, from Late Latin mātrimōnium ad morganāticam, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning-gift”).

First attested in the 13th c. Inherited from Middle French moriginer (“to educate, rear”), derived from Old French moriginé (“well-mannered, well-behaved”), borrowed from Medieval Latin mōrigenātus (“endowed with good character, good-natured”), from mōrigenus, formed as a variant of classical mōrige
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin mortuarius.

Inherited from Old French mote (“mound”), from Medieval Latin mota (“a mound, hill”), of Germanic origin, perhaps via Frankish *mot, *motta (“mud, peat, bog, turf”), from Proto-Germanic *mutô, *mudraz, *muþraz (“dirt, filth, mud, swamp”).

Inherited from Middle French moufle, from Old French mofle (“thick glove”), from Medieval Latin muffula (817, Carolingian), a Germanic borrowing from Frankish *molfell (“soft garment made of hide”), from *mol (“softened, forworn”) + *fell (“hide, skin”), from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz (“tender, soft”
Borrowed from Medieval Latin mulsiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin mūsicālis. By surface analysis, musique + -al.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin myrtillus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin medicālis (compare Classical Latin medicīnālis, whence the French médicinal), from Latin medicus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin meditativus. By surface analysis, méditer + -atif.
Medieval Latin mellācea, mellāceum.
Inherited from Middle French Merovinge, borrowed from Medieval Latin Merovingus, from Proto-West Germanic *Mārīwīg or *-ing. By surface analysis, Mérovée + -inge.

parole.significato: tit, chickadee, titmouse (any of a large number of small tree-dwelling passerine birds)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French mésange, from Old French mesenge, masenge (“titmouse”), from Medieval Latin misinga and spelling variants, from Frankish *meisinga (“titmouse”) and variants, from Proto-Germanic *maisǭ (“titmouse”), *-ingō (“-ing”). Cognate with Old High German meisa (“titmouse”), Old En
Inherited from Old French meslee, older meslede, from the feminine past participle of early Medieval Latin misculō, derived from Latin misceō. By surface analysis, mêl- + -ée.
Inherited from Old French narcotique, borrowed from Medieval Latin narcōticus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nāsālis, from Latin nāsus (“nose”).
From Medieval Latin nōtōrius, from Latin nōtus (“known”), past participle of nōscere (“to get to know”).

parole.significato: numerator (number or expression written above the line in a fraction)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French numerateur, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin numerātōr.
Inherited from Middle French nuque, nuche, borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin necessitāre (“to oblige, compel”), from Classical Latin necessitās (“necessity, compulsion”) (whence nécessité). According to the Trésor de la langue française, attested by the 14th century.
From Medieval Latin nenuphar, from Arabic نِلُوفَر (nilūfar), نِينُوفَر (nīnūfar), from Middle Persian nylw(k)pl (nīlōpal, “lotus, water-lily”), from Sanskrit नीलोत्पल (nīlotpala, “blue lotus”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin obituārius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin obiectum.

parole.significato: Occitan (an endangered Romance language spoken in Occitania, a region of Europe that includes Southern France, Auvergne…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Occitānus in the phrase lingua Occitāna, Latinization of langue d'oc. The ending -itanus perhaps after aquitanus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin offerta.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin officiō (infinitive officiāre).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin officiārius.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin offerenda, from Latin offerendus (literally “to be offered”), gerundive of offerō (“to offer”). Compare Catalan ofrena, Occitan and Romansh ufrenda, Portuguese oferenda, Spanish ofrenda.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin olibanum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin oleāginōsus.
From Medieval Latin oleandru, from Late Latin lorandrum, perhaps an alteration of rhododendron.
From Medieval Latin omniscientia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omniscientem (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciēns (“knowing”).
Inherited from Old French orillier. By surface analysis, oreille + -ier. Cf. also Medieval Latin auriculāre, substantivized form of Latin auriculāris. Doublet of auriculaire.

parole.significato: to organise; to plan an event
parole.testo: From Middle French organiser, borrowed from Medieval Latin organizāre.
Inherited from Old French oriflamme, orie flambe, from Medieval Latin auriflamma (“golden flame”), from Latin aurum (“gold”) + flamma.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin orthogōnālis, from Latin orthogōnius (“right-angled”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ovālis.
Inherited from Old French palefreid, from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin palefredus, variant of Late Latin paraveredus.
From Medieval Latin palliātīvus, from Latin palliō (“I conceal”).

parole.significato: Feeding of pigs on beech nuts and acorns in the forests
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French and Old French pasnage, from Medieval Latin pāstiōnāticum (“the right to feed on mast”).

parole.significato: sign, placard (with a message on it, such as might be carried during a protest)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pancharta.

parole.significato: to panify, to turn into bread
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin panificāre; not found in Middle or Old French as such, but compare Old French panegier.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin papālis. By surface analysis, pape + -al.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin paradoxum, from Latin paradoxa (“things contrary to expectation”), from Ancient Greek παράδοξα (parádoxa).
Inherited from Old French parement, from Medieval Latin parāmentum, from parō (“adorn”) + -mentum.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin parentheticus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin partītīvus, from Latin partītus + -īvus.
Secondary to passe-fleur, and parallelly to it from Medieval Latin rosa passiōnis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin patristica, from Latin pater (“father”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin peccaminōsus. By surface analysis, Latin peccāmen (“sin”) + -eux.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin perclūsus (“obstructed”), past participle of perclūdō (“to seal shut”) (infinitive perclūdere).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).
Inherited from Old French farmacie, borrowed from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).
Calque of Medieval Latin pia māter.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin pilula, apparently first attested in the fourteenth century, in turn inherited from the Classical Latin, attested in the medical sense in Pliny. Note that Italian pillola and Spanish píldora are widely regarded as inheritances, not borrowings.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pinnāculum. Doublet of panache.
Inherited from Old French pitance, pitence, from Medieval Latin *pietāntia, from Latin pietās (“piety”).
From Medieval Latin Pedemontem, from Latin ad pedem montium. By surface analysis, pied (“foot”) + -mont (“hill”).
Inherited from Old French plainte, pleinte (from the feminine past participle of plaindre, pleindre), corresponding to a Medieval Latin plancta, from Latin planctus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin planta (of the same origin as the above etymology), or possibly partly derived from the verb planter. Doublet of clan.

parole.significato: of a pole (of an axis); polar
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French polaire, from Medieval Latin polāris (“relating to poles”), from Latin polus (“pole or end of an axis”), from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “sky, pivot or axis of a sphere”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolo- (“turn around”), from *kʷel- (“to move around, to roll or wheel”)
Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuālis, from punctus (whence French point).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuāre, from Latin punctus.

parole.significato: practical, applied (concerning action or intervention of human will on the real to change it)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French practique, from Medieval Latin prāctica.
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin prōmissa (“promise”), from Latin prōmissum (“promise”), from promittō (“to send forth; to promise”).

Inherited from Middle French prognostic, borrowed from Medieval Latin prognōsticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from προ- (pro-, “before”) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “relating to knowledge”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to be aware of, perceive, observe, know, learn”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsiōnem, from Latin propulsus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prosaicus, from Latin prosa.

parole.significato: prosimetrum (a poetic composition consisting of both prose and verse, usually in alternation)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prosimetrum.

From Middle French protocolle, protocole (“document, record”), from Medieval Latin prōtocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos, “first

parole.significato: preamble (a short statement or remark, especially an explanatory introduction to a formal document or statute)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French preambule, borrowed from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from Late Latin praeambulō.
Inherited from Middle French, from Medieval Latin preconizō, praeconizāre, from Latin praecō (“crier, herald”, noun).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin praedīlēctiō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin praeēmptiō (“previous purchase”).

Inherited from Old French preface, borrowed from Medieval Latin prefatia, from Classical Latin praefātiō (“preface, prologue”), from praefor (“to speak beforehand”), from prae- (“beforehand”) + for (“to speak”).
From Old French prelat, from Medieval Latin praelatus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin praemissa (prōpositiō) (“proposition set before”).
From président + -ence, or a borrowing from Medieval Latin praesidentia. See also préséance.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūblicitātem, itself constructed from pūblicus (“public”) + -tās (noun-forming suffix).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pulmōnicus, from pulmō (“lung”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnitīvus, from pūniō (“to punish”).

parole.significato: purgatory (stage of the afterlife in Catholic theology)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūrgātōrium (“cleansing”). By surface analysis, purger + -atoire.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pediluvium.
From Medieval Latin petroleum, from petra (“rock”) + oleum (“oil”).
Inherited from Middle French qualification, from Medieval Latin quālificātiō.
From quart + -ier, possibly Medieval Latin quarterium, compare also Latin quartārium; cognate with Italian quartiere.

parole.significato: quiddity (essence or inherent nature of a person or thing; that which makes something what it is)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin quidditas.

parole.significato: quintal, a nonstandard metric unit of mass equivalent to exactly 100 kg
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French quintal, from Medieval Latin quintāle (“various medieval hundredweights”), from Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār, “100 rottols”), from Classical Syriac ܩܰܢܛܺܝܪܳܐ (qanṭīrā) and ܩܰܢܛܺܝܢܳܪܳܐ (qanṭīnārā), from Byzantine Greek κεντηνάριον (kentēnárion), from Latin centēnārium (“100 Roman
Univerbation of quinte essence, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin quinta essentia.
Extracted from the Medieval Latin phrase dispūtātiōnes de quōlibet.
Inherited from Old French ramifier, borrowed from Medieval Latin ramificāre, from Latin ramus (“branch”) + facio (“to do”).

parole.significato: to repatriate; to send home (to send back to the country of origin)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin repatriāre, repatriō, with substitution of the prefix re- by ra-. Doublet of repairer.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rārēfactiōnem, from rarefaciō (“to rarefy”).
From Medieval Latin ratificare, from Latin ratus (“established, authoritative; fixed, certain”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin rectangulum.
Inherited from Middle French registre, from Medieval Latin registrum.
Inherited from Middle French remonstrance, from Medieval Latin remōnstrantia. By surface analysis, remontrer + -ance.

From Old French remors, from Medieval Latin remorsus, from Latin remordeō (“to torment, to vex”, literally “to bite back”), from re- + mordeō (“to bite”). The d was added later by analogy with remordre.
From Medieval Latin repraesentātīvus.

parole.significato: respective (referencing two or more things as individuals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin respectivus, from Latin respectus. Equivalent to respect + -if.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin rotātōrius, from Classical Latin rotō. Cognate to Catalan rotatori, Italian and Spanish rotatorio, Portuguese rotatório.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rotula.
Inherited from Old French rubi, rubin, borrowed from Medieval Latin rubinus, from Latin rubeus.

parole.significato: reaction (action in response to an event)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reactio.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitās, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”). Morphologically, from réel + -ité.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin repertōrium.
Formed from Latin repulsus with the French suffix -if, or borrowed from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin resultātum, the substantivized neuter singular of resultātus (perfect passive participle of resultō). By surface analysis, résulter + -at.

parole.significato: retina (thin layer of cells at the back of the eyeball)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin rētīna (“small net”), a diminutive of rēte.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin sāl petrae, from sāl (“salt”) and petra (“rock, stone”).

parole.significato: sandalwood (any of various trees in genus Santalum; the aromatic wood of such trees)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin santalum, sandalum, from Byzantine Greek σάνταλον (sántalon), from Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Sassanidae.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin similāris, extended from Latin similis (“like”).

From Old French sirop, borrowed from Medieval Latin siroppus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “beverage”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”).
From the stem of Medieval Latin sirupus + -eux.

parole.significato: to locate (to find the location of something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin situāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sōlemnizāre, from Latin sollemnis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin somnambulus (“sleepwalker”), from Latin somnus (“sleep”) + ambulō (“to walk”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin sophisticāre (“to trick, falsify, corrupt”). The sense "to make more complex" is probably due to later developments in sophistiqué, influenced by changes in sense in English sophisticated.
Inherited from Old French, from Medieval Latin sortilegium, from Latin sortilegus (“sorcerer, diviner”), from sors (“sort”) + legere (“choose”).

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin specificāre, from specificus (“specific, particular”), from Latin speciēs (“kind, quality, species”) (whence espèce).

parole.significato: internship, job that a trainee is doing in a workplace until a fixed date
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stagium, itself from Old French estage: ester + -age (whence modern French étage).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stagiārius, from stagium + -ārius. By surface analysis, stage + -aire.
From Medieval Latin stallum.

parole.significato: to stigmatize (to mark with a permanent identity mark branded, cut or tattooed onto the skin)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin stigmatizō, from Byzantine Greek στιγματίζω (stigmatízō). By surface analysis, stigmate + -iser.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin subornatio. By surface analysis, suborner + -ation.

parole.significato: to subsume (to place under another as belonging to it)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin subsūmere, from sub- + sūmō (“take”).
From Middle French subterfuge m, borrowed from Medieval Latin subterfugium n, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugio (“to flee”).
From Medieval Latin sultānātus, from sultānus + -ātus. By surface analysis, sultan + -at.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin superioritātem, from Latin superior. By surface analysis, supérieur + -ité.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sebesten, from Arabic سِبِسْتَان (sibistān), from Persian سگپستان (sag-pestân, from سگ (sag, “dog”) + پستان (pestân, “teat”), literally “dog teat”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sedātīvus, from sedō.

From Old French segraierie, from segraier (whence ségrayer (“a forest official”)) + -ie, from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius (“an officer charged with forestry duties, a forest official”), from Latin sēcrētus (“separated, taken apart”).

From Old French segraier (whence ségrayer (“a forest official”)), from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius (“an officer charged with forestry duties, a forest official”), from Latin sēcrētus (“separated, taken apart”).

parole.significato: the administrator of a ségrairie (a woodland held in common)
parole.testo: From Old French segraier, from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius (“an officer charged with forestry duties, a forest official”), from Latin sēcrētus (“separated, taken apart”).
Inherited from Middle French tamarin, from earlier tamarinde, from Old French tamarinde, from Medieval Latin tamarindus, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ (tamr hindiyy).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin tara or Italian tara, from Arabic طَرْح (ṭarḥ, “rubbish, refuse”), from طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “to reject, to deduct”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Tartarus, alteration of Tatar, from a Turkic name. Influenced by Tartarus (“underworld”).
Inherited from Middle French temporiser, a borrowing from Medieval Latin temporizāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tendō.

parole.significato: attempt, try, effort (particularly of something difficult or risky)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin tentātīva, from tentō (“to attempt”).

Inherited from Old French, from Medieval Latin terrārius (“of earth”) from Latin terra (“earth”); or equivalent to terre + -ier. Most terrier breeds were developed to hunt vermin both over and under the ground.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin thuriferarius, from Latin thurifer.

From Medieval Latin theosophus (“a theologian”, noun), from Koine Greek θεόσοφος (theósophos, “wise in things concerning god”, adjective), from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”) + σοφός (sophós, “wise”). Cognate to Spanish teósofo (noun).
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin tunna, tonna, itself from a Celtic word cognate to Irish tonn.
From Middle French total (14th c.), a borrowing from Medieval Latin tōtālis.
From transparent + -ence, or borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentia, from trānspārēns (“transparent”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentem (“transparent”), present participle of transpareō, from Latin trāns + pareō.

parole.significato: transpiration (process of giving off water vapour through the skin or mucous membranes)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trānspirātiō. By surface analysis, transpirer + -ation.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspirāre, from Latin trāns + spiro.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trānsversālis, from Latin trānsversus (whence transverse and travers).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin tritonus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τρίτονος (trítonos). By surface analysis, tri- + ton.
Inherited from Old French trot, troter, from Medieval Latin trottare, of Germanic origin.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin trepanum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “auger, drill”).

From typographe + -ie, from Medieval Latin typographia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ubīquitās (“ubiquity, omnipresence”).
Inherited from Old French universitei, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin universitātem.
From Middle French usage, from Old French usage. By surface analysis, user + -age. Compare Medieval Latin usagium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Usnea.

parole.significato: a male attendant of a knight or a lord
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French vaslet, from Medieval Latin *vassellittus, diminutive of Late Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).

Inherited from Middle French valise, from Medieval Latin valesia, valixia, from Late Latin valisia, possibly from Gaulish *valisia (“leather bag”), from Proto-Celtic *val- (“to enclose, surround”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Or, possibly from Arabic وَلِيهَة (walīha, “large bag”). Maybe a borr
Borrowed from Medieval Latin variābilitātem, from Latin variābilis (“variable”), from variō (“to vary”) (from varius (“varied, different, spotted”)) + -bilis (“-able”).

From Middle French vassal, from Old French vassal, from Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).
Inherited from Old French vavasour, from Medieval Latin vavassor.

parole.significato: velleity (weak or vacillating desire to do something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin velleitātem, from velle (“to will”).
Inherited from Middle French ventouse, from Old French ventuse, ellipsis of Medieval Latin [cucurbita] ventōsa. Doublet of venteux and ventôse.

parole.significato: version; model (a specific state, variant, or form of something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French version, from Medieval Latin versiōnem (“turning, rendition”), from Latin vertō (“turn”).
From Old French visconte, reduced form of Old French vice conte, from Medieval Latin vicecomes, < Latin vices comes. See vice- and comte.

Compare Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula). Possibly ultimately from Medieval Latin vitula. Compare also Catalan, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish viola, Spanish vihuela. Doublet of viole, borrowed from the Old Occitan. See also English fiddle.

parole.significato: to vilipend, vilify, revile, scorn, despise, condemn
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin vīlipendō, from vīlis (“vile”) and pendō (“to weigh; to consider”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin virtuālis.
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vitrōsus (“glassy, transparent”), from vitrum (“glass”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vitriolum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin volitiōnem (“will, volition”), from Latin volō (“to wish, to will”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.
From Old French vegetatif or Medieval Latin vegetātīvus, from Latin vegetatus.

parole.significato: Venetian (of, from or relating to the city of Venice in the Veneto region, Italy)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French Venicien, from Medieval Latin Venetianus, from Latin Venetia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vērificāre, from Latin vērus (“true”) + faciō (“to do, to make”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vayrola, from Latin variola.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin zerumbet, zurumbet, zurumbeth, from Arabic زُرُنْبَاد (zurunbād), from Persian زرنباد (zoronbâd).

From Medieval Latin scaccārium, from Vulgar Latin *scaccus, itself from Persian. See exchequer.

parole.significato: schoolmaster of a medieval cathedral school
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin scholastrum, from Latin scholasticus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ēditiōnem.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios). Cognate to Old French ypidime.

PIE word  *nókʷts From Old French equinoce, from Medieval Latin equinoxium, from Latin aequinoctium, from aequus (“equal”) + nox (“night”).
From Medieval Latin aequivalentia.

parole.significato: muslin, cheesecloth, etamine (a fine fabric often used to filter liquids)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin stāminea (“kind of woollen cloth”), from stāmineus (“trimmed with thread”), from Latin stāmen (“warp (of a loom)”). The biological sense is by etymological analogy.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hecticus, from Ancient Greek ἑκτικός (hektikós).
